source: It also lets you want suffering to end without that wish turning into desperation or fear of failure.

neighbors.lead: In the Metta Sutta, you wish ease and happiness to beings, yourself included. Metta calms the hindrances and builds goodwill.
neighbors.end: Theravada and most Mahayana Buddhist traditions treat metta as essential groundwork before the deeper work of unweaving the sense streams that make up the mind.

protected_claims: The claim is about the *wish* for suffering to end
Metta changes how the wish is held, not a blanket cure or generic permission
The wish does not become desperation
The wish does not become fear of failure
No claims of personal experience or of medical efficacy may be invented
known_failed_repair: An earlier attempt changed the actor from wish to person and kept formulaic lets-you-X-without-Y cadence; fresh critic marked meaning uncertain; no Pangram call was used on that.

prompts.title: Begin with the lived paradox
prompts.prompt:
You are writing a sentence or two in an idiosyncratic, intelligent first-person Buddhist meditation essay, between two existing owner-written passages. Never change those surrounding lines. The author has a SPECIFIC distinct claim to convey: mettā makes it possible to wish for suffering to end without that *wish itself* turning into desperation or fear of failure. It is not a generic permission to feel hopeful, a promise to end suffering, a story about the author, or a reason to doubt sincere desire. Keep wish/aspiration the conceptual subject; keep both desperation and fear of failure. There is no permission to invent doctrine, examples, autobiography, risk advice or new claims. This is a substantive voice task, not a word synonym task. Do not imitate a template or turn it into a mini-essay with a moral. Write exactly the needed reader-facing passage, 20–50 words. No headings, analysis, source notes, citations or tool use.

UNCHANGED PRECEDING PROSE:
In the Metta Sutta, you wish ease and happiness to beings, yourself included. Metta calms the hindrances and builds goodwill.

UNCHANGED FOLLOWING PROSE:
Theravada and most Mahayana Buddhist traditions treat metta as essential groundwork before the deeper work of unweaving the sense streams that make up the mind.

AUTHORIAL CLAIM:
Mettā allows the desire for suffering to end to remain caring, rather than the wish itself escalating into desperation or fear of failing to end suffering.

Composition premise: the reader recognizes how a well-meant wish can itself become a source of suffering when someone starts desperately needing a result. Follow that lived tension before naming how mettā affects the wish. No new abstract explanation. Output ONLY the insert.
